prompt: What does HLS stand for?
options: HTTP Live Streaming
High-Latency Segmenting
HTML Layered Streams
Hybrid Linear Service
explanation: HLS is Apple's HTTP Live Streaming protocol, specified in RFC 8216.

prompt: Which file extension does an HLS playlist use?
options: .m3u8
.mpd
.ism
.f4m
explanation: HLS playlists are UTF-8 M3U files with the .m3u8 extension. .mpd is DASH.

prompt: What is a DASH manifest called?
options: An MPD (Media Presentation Description), written in XML
An M3U8 playlist, written as plain text lines with EXT tags
A SMIL file describing timed media clips
A JSON index generated by the packager
explanation: MPEG-DASH describes a presentation with an XML MPD document.

prompt: Which company created HLS?
options: Apple
Google
Microsoft
Netflix
explanation: Apple introduced HLS in 2009 for iPhone OS 3.

prompt: What does adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming do?
options: Switches between renditions of different quality as conditions change
Compresses each downloaded segment further whenever the network is slow
Lowers the frame rate of one fixed rendition under load
Downloads the whole file first, then picks a quality
explanation: The player picks among pre-encoded renditions based on bandwidth, buffer and device.

prompt: Why does segmented HTTP delivery work well with CDNs?
options: Segments are ordinary cacheable HTTP files
CDNs transcode each segment for every viewer
Segments stream over a persistent UDP socket
Each viewer gets a private encrypted connection
explanation: Every segment is a normal HTTP object, so standard web caches can serve it.

prompt: What does an HLS multivariant (master) playlist list?
options: The available variant streams with bandwidth, resolution and codecs
Every media segment of the default rendition in order
The DRM license server and its key rotation schedule
The ad breaks and their SCTE-35 cue positions
explanation: It points to one media playlist per variant and describes each one.

prompt: What does an HLS media playlist contain?
options: The ordered segment URIs for one rendition
The list of all renditions and their bitrates
The license request needed for playback
The player's buffer and bitrate settings
explanation: A media playlist is the segment sequence for a single rendition.

prompt: What is rebuffering?
options: Playback stalls because the buffer has run empty
The player downloads segments ahead of the playhead on purpose
The player switches to a higher rendition
The first segment loads before the play button
explanation: A stall happens when there is no buffered media left to render.

prompt: What does time to first frame measure?
options: The delay from the play request to the first rendered frame
The time the encoder takes to produce the first segment of a stream
The duration of the first segment in the playlist
The time between two keyframes in the stream
explanation: TTFF (startup time) is a core viewer-experience metric.

prompt: What is the job of DRM in streaming?
options: Allowing decryption only for licensed players under policy
Compressing content so it is harder to copy
Hiding segment URLs from the browser's network tab and dev tools
Watermarking each frame with the viewer's email
explanation: Content is encrypted, and a license grants a device the keys and usage rules.

prompt: Which DRM system does Apple use?
options: FairPlay Streaming
Widevine
PlayReady
Marlin
explanation: Apple platforms use FairPlay Streaming.

prompt: Which DRM system is Google's?
options: Widevine
FairPlay Streaming
PlayReady
PrimeTime
explanation: Widevine is Google's DRM, used in Chrome, Android and many TVs.

prompt: Which DRM system is Microsoft's?
options: PlayReady
Widevine
FairPlay Streaming
ClearKey
explanation: PlayReady is Microsoft's DRM, common on Edge, Xbox and smart TVs.

prompt: What is server-side ad insertion (SSAI)?
options: Stitching ads into the stream so the player sees one continuous stream
Letting the player request ads and play them through a separate player instance
Showing banner ads next to the player on the page
Encoding ads into the original content master file
explanation: SSAI modifies the manifest so ad segments appear inline with content.

prompt: What is client-side ad insertion (CSAI)?
options: The player itself requests ads and switches to play them
The origin stitches ad segments into the manifest before delivery
The CDN replaces content segments with ads
The encoder burns ads into the live feed
explanation: In CSAI an ad SDK in the client fetches and plays ads around content.

prompt: In ABR, what is a rendition?
options: One encoding of the content at a given bitrate and resolution
One segment of the content stored at the highest available quality
A copy of the content stored on another CDN
A different language edition of the same title
explanation: A set of renditions forms the bitrate ladder.

prompt: What is hls.js?
options: A JavaScript library that plays HLS in browsers using MSE
A native Safari API for decoding HLS
A server that packages video into HLS
A browser extension that downloads HLS streams for offline viewing
explanation: hls.js parses playlists, fetches segments and feeds them to Media Source Extensions.

prompt: Which browser has supported HLS natively in the video element since HLS launched?
options: Safari
Chrome
Firefox
Opera
explanation: Safari has played HLS natively from the start; other browsers long needed an MSE library such as hls.js.

prompt: How does an HLS VOD playlist show that it is complete?
options: It ends with the EXT-X-ENDLIST tag
It sets EXT-X-TARGETDURATION to zero
It omits the EXTM3U header
It lists a segment with duration -1
explanation: EXT-X-ENDLIST says no more segments will be added.

prompt: Which subtitle format is standard for web video tracks?
options: WebVTT
SRT only
SCC
TTML only
explanation: WebVTT is the format of the HTML track element and HLS subtitle renditions.

prompt: What does rebuffer ratio express?
options: Time spent stalled as a share of total viewing time
Number of bitrate switches per minute
Share of segments fetched from the CDN cache instead of the origin
Ratio of audio to video buffer length
explanation: It normalizes stall time by session length so sessions compare fairly.

prompt: What role does a CDN play in video delivery?
options: Caching and serving segments close to viewers
Encoding the source into multiple bitrates for ABR
Issuing DRM licenses to authorized players
Deciding which ad plays in each break
explanation: CDNs offload origin and cut latency by serving from edge caches.

prompt: What is Shaka Player?
options: Google's open-source JavaScript player for DASH and HLS
Apple's native player framework for tvOS
A commercial live encoder for broadcast
A CDN feature for segment prefetching
explanation: Shaka Player is maintained by Google and supports DASH, HLS and EME.

prompt: What is Media3 ExoPlayer?
options: Google's media playback library for Android
Apple's native playback framework for iOS and tvOS apps
A web player built on hls.js
A server that converts DASH to HLS
explanation: ExoPlayer now ships as part of AndroidX Media3.

prompt: What do Media Source Extensions (MSE) let JavaScript do?
options: Append media bytes to SourceBuffers that feed a video element
Decrypt protected media with a license key
Decode video frames in a Web Worker
Open a direct UDP socket to the CDN
explanation: MSE lets script build the media stream that the video element plays.

prompt: What do Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) provide?
options: An API connecting the video element to a platform decryption module
A way to encrypt segments in the browser before uploading them to origin
A standard DRM system shared by every browser
A JavaScript implementation of Widevine
explanation: EME lets web apps negotiate licenses with a CDM; the DRM itself stays in the platform.

prompt: What is a CDM (content decryption module)?
options: The platform component that holds keys and decrypts protected media
The server that issues DRM licenses
The packager step that encrypts segments
The browser cache for decrypted segments
explanation: The CDM (for example Widevine in Chrome) does the actual decryption.

prompt: What does EXT-X-TARGETDURATION declare?
options: The maximum segment duration in the playlist, in whole seconds
The exact duration of every segment
How long the player should buffer before it starts playing the stream
The total duration of the VOD asset
explanation: Each segment's duration, rounded to the nearest integer, must not exceed it.

prompt: What is the live edge?
options: The newest point in a live stream that can be played
The first segment in the live playlist window
The moment the broadcast is scheduled to end
The highest-bitrate rendition available in a live stream
explanation: Players usually hold a safe distance behind it.

prompt: What limits the DVR window of a live HLS stream?
options: How many segments the live playlist keeps
The player's maximum forward buffer length setting in seconds
The CDN's cache TTL for segments
The DRM license duration
explanation: Viewers can only seek to segments still listed in the playlist.

prompt: Why do many players start on a lower rendition?
options: There is no bandwidth estimate yet, and startup speed matters
Lower renditions are always cached at the CDN
DRM licenses only cover low quality at first
Browsers forbid HD before user interaction
explanation: A cautious first pick shortens startup; ABR climbs once it has measurements.

prompt: What does a buffer-based ABR algorithm such as BOLA use?
options: How much media is currently buffered
Only the last segment's download speed
The viewer's subscription tier
The CDN's reported cache hit ratio
explanation: BOLA picks bitrates from buffer occupancy rather than throughput predictions.

prompt: Why can always choosing the highest bitrate hurt experience?
options: Stalls from a draining buffer cost more than slightly lower quality
High bitrates increase DRM license failures
Browsers throttle high-bitrate video in background tabs and windows
CDNs refuse to cache high-bitrate segments
explanation: Viewers are more annoyed by stalls than by a small resolution drop.

prompt: What is CMAF?
options: A fragmented MP4 format that both HLS and DASH can reference
A DRM system shared by Apple and Google
An ad-insertion signaling standard
A new codec replacing H.264
explanation: One set of CMAF segments can serve both HLS and DASH manifests.

prompt: What does Common Encryption (CENC) standardize?
options: How content is encrypted so one file works with several DRM systems
One license server protocol for all DRM vendors
A browser API for choosing a DRM system
A replacement for FairPlay on Apple devices
explanation: ISO/IEC 23001-7 defines shared encryption schemes and signaling.

prompt: Why should each segment start with a keyframe?
options: So it can be decoded without earlier segments, enabling switching and seeking
So the CDN can compress it more efficiently
So DRM licenses can be scoped per segment
So subtitles stay in sync with audio
explanation: An IDR frame at each boundary makes segments independently decodable.

prompt: Why can a player switch renditions without restarting playback?
options: Aligned segments let it fetch the next one from another rendition
Every rendition shares one media file
The CDN switches the quality transparently
The decoder rescales one rendition on the fly
explanation: With aligned boundaries, the next segment can come from any rendition.

prompt: What does SCTE-35 signal in a live stream?
options: Where ad breaks or other program events start and end
Which DRM key protects each segment
The bitrate of each rendition
The subtitle language of each track
explanation: SCTE-35 cue messages mark ad opportunities for insertion systems.

prompt: What is VAST?
options: An IAB XML format describing an ad, its media files and tracking URLs
A streaming protocol designed for ads
A DRM scheme used only for ad content
A CDN routing standard for ad segments
explanation: Ad servers return VAST so players know what to play and which beacons to fire.

prompt: Why is SSAI harder for ad blockers to skip?
options: Ad segments arrive in the same stream and from the same domain as content
SSAI encrypts ads with a separate DRM key
Ad blockers cannot run on streaming apps at all
SSAI ads are rendered by the operating system
explanation: There is no separate ad request for a blocker to filter.

prompt: What does personalized SSAI do to CDN caching?
options: Manifests become per-viewer, while ad and content segments stay shared
Segments can no longer be cached at all
Every segment has to be encrypted per viewer
Only the highest rendition can be cached
explanation: Each session gets its own manifest; the segments themselves are reusable.

prompt: With SSAI, why do players often still send ad beacons?
options: Only the device knows whether the ad was actually played and seen
Servers cannot parse VAST tracking URLs
Beacons are required to decrypt ad segments
The CDN blocks server-to-server requests
explanation: Client-side beacons confirm real playback for advertiser measurement.

prompt: How does Chromecast playback work in a typical sender app?
options: The sender tells a receiver app on the device what to load, and the device fetches the stream
The phone streams decoded video frames to the device
The device mirrors the phone's screen
The CDN pushes segments to the device on a schedule
explanation: The Cast receiver plays media itself; the sender acts as a remote.

prompt: Which adaptive streaming format does AVPlayer support natively?
options: HTTP Live Streaming (HLS)
MPEG-DASH
Microsoft Smooth Streaming
Adobe HTTP Dynamic Streaming
explanation: Apple's AVFoundation plays HLS natively; DASH requires a custom solution.

prompt: What do many dropped frames usually indicate?
options: The device cannot decode or render fast enough
The network is too slow for the rendition that was selected
The CDN is serving stale segments
The DRM license has expired
explanation: Dropped frames point to device performance, not throughput.

prompt: What does 'exit before video start' capture?
options: Viewers who leave while the video is still starting
Viewers who stop watching within the first minute of playback
Sessions that failed with a fatal error
Viewers who skipped the pre-roll ad
explanation: It exposes startup pain that failure counts miss.

prompt: Why should playback error events carry a category?
options: So network, manifest, media and DRM failures can be triaged separately
So the player can hide errors from viewers
So errors can be retried in the right order
So the CDN can bill errors per category
explanation: Different categories have different owners and fixes.

prompt: What does the HLS CODECS attribute let a player do?
options: Skip variants whose codecs the device cannot decode
Pick the DRM system for the stream
Decide how long each segment is
Choose the subtitle language
explanation: Players can check support (for example with MediaSource.isTypeSupported) before fetching.

prompt: How does hls.js keep a small player from fetching 4K?
options: It can cap the level to the player's size
It always downloads the lowest rendition in small players
It asks the CDN to downscale segments
It only reads the first variant listed
explanation: capLevelToPlayerSize limits renditions to what the element can show.

prompt: What does a Low-Latency HLS partial segment (EXT-X-PART) allow?
options: Fetching parts of a segment before the whole segment is finished
Splitting a VOD file into parallel downloads
Encrypting only part of a segment
Skipping segments that contain ads
explanation: Parts shorten the wait for new media, cutting latency.

prompt: What is LL-HLS blocking playlist reload?
options: The client asks for a future update and the server holds the response until it exists
The player blocks playback until the playlist is complete
The CDN blocks reloads faster than the target duration
The server refuses playlist requests during ad breaks
explanation: Requests with _HLS_msn and _HLS_part avoid polling delays.

prompt: What does EXT-X-PRELOAD-HINT tell a Low-Latency HLS client?
options: The URI of the next part so it can request it early
Which rendition to start with
When the stream will end
Which DRM license to prefetch
explanation: The client can issue the request before the part is published.

prompt: How does low-latency DASH usually deliver segments?
options: As CMAF chunks sent with HTTP chunked transfer encoding
As whole segments pushed over WebSockets
As MPEG-TS packets over UDP multicast
As one long MP4 file with range requests
explanation: Chunks arrive while the segment is still being encoded.

prompt: Where does RFC 8216 say an HLS live client should start?
options: Not less than three target durations from the end of the playlist
Always at the first segment in the playlist
Exactly at the last segment
At the segment tagged EXT-X-START only
explanation: This keeps enough media ahead of the playhead to avoid stalls.

prompt: Why do longer segments usually mean higher live latency?
options: Players keep several segments of distance from the live edge
Longer segments take longer to decrypt
CDNs cache longer segments for longer
Encoders only emit keyframes at segment ends
explanation: Latency scales with segment duration times the segments held back.

prompt: What does EXT-X-DISCONTINUITY signal?
options: A change in encoding or timestamps, such as a switch to an ad
A missing segment the player should skip
The end of the DVR window
A new DRM key for the next segment
explanation: Players reset their timestamp expectations at the boundary.

prompt: What is EXT-X-PROGRAM-DATE-TIME used for?
options: Mapping segments to wall-clock time
Setting the segment's cache expiry
Scheduling when a VOD becomes available
Declaring the license expiry time
explanation: It enables EPG sync, ad timing and cross-device alignment.

prompt: Why do ABR controllers smooth bandwidth samples, for example with an EWMA?
options: Single downloads are noisy, and raw samples cause oscillation
Raw samples cannot be measured in browsers
Smoothing makes segments download faster
The CDN requires averaged request rates
explanation: hls.js combines fast and slow EWMAs for a stable estimate.

prompt: Why add hysteresis to ABR up-switches?
options: To avoid visible oscillation between two renditions
To slow down startup on purpose
To keep the forward buffer as small as possible at all times
To reduce DRM license requests
explanation: Requiring headroom before switching up prevents flip-flopping.

prompt: What separates Widevine L1 from L3?
options: L1 decrypts and decodes in a hardware trusted environment; L3 is software only
L1 is for audio and L3 is for video
L1 works offline and L3 only online
L1 is Android only and L3 is browser only
explanation: Many services restrict HD and higher to L1 devices.

prompt: What does HDCP protect?
options: The link from the device to the display
The license request between the player and the DRM server
The segment download from the CDN
The decryption key inside the CDM
explanation: DRM policy can require HDCP before output at high resolutions.

prompt: Why rotate content keys on long live streams?
options: A leaked key only exposes a limited window
Rotation makes segments smaller
Players cannot cache a key longer than a segment
Rotation reduces the manifest size
explanation: Periodic key changes cap the damage of a compromised key.

prompt: Why is the cbcs encryption mode popular with CMAF?
options: FairPlay and modern Widevine and PlayReady all support it, so one asset serves all
It encrypts audio only, which lowers CPU cost
It removes the need for a license server
It is the only mode supported by hls.js
explanation: A single cbcs-encrypted asset can reach Apple and non-Apple devices.

prompt: What does QuotaExceededError on SourceBuffer.appendBuffer mean?
options: The media buffer is full, so older ranges must be removed
The license quota for the device has been used up for the day
The CDN rejected the segment request
The video element ran out of GPU memory
explanation: Players evict already-played ranges before appending more.

prompt: What should a player do about a small gap in its buffered ranges?
options: Jump over it so playback does not stall forever
Restart the whole session
Reload the DRM license
Switch to the lowest rendition permanently to refill the buffer
explanation: Shaka and hls.js include gap-jumping logic.

prompt: What prevents leaks when a web player switches streams with hls.js?
options: Calling destroy() on the old instance to release MediaSource and listeners
Setting the video element's src to the new URL only
Pausing the old stream before loading the next
Clearing the browser's HTTP cache
explanation: destroy() detaches media and tears down loaders and events.

prompt: Why is buffering after a seek usually excluded from rebuffer ratio?
options: The viewer caused it, so it isn't a delivery problem
Seek buffering cannot be measured
Seeks only happen in VOD
Seek buffering is always shorter than a second, so it is noise
explanation: Rebuffer metrics target involuntary stalls; seek wait is tracked separately.

prompt: Why report startup time as percentiles rather than an average?
options: A few very slow starts disappear in an average
Averages cannot be computed across devices and platform versions
Percentiles use less storage
The average is always equal to the median
explanation: p95 and p99 show the tail that viewers complain about.

prompt: What does HLS Content Steering (EXT-X-CONTENT-STEERING) allow?
options: A server to tell players which pathway or CDN to prefer, during playback
Players to pick subtitles by region
The encoder to steer bitrates per viewer
The CDN to rewrite manifests for ads
explanation: A steering manifest can move traffic between CDNs mid-session.

prompt: What are HLS I-frame playlists (EXT-X-I-FRAME-STREAM-INF) for?
options: Fast scrubbing and trick play using keyframes only
Storing all ad creatives separately
Delivering audio-only renditions
Providing the DRM license URLs
explanation: They reference keyframes so players can preview while seeking.

prompt: How does HLS offer alternate audio languages?
options: EXT-X-MEDIA TYPE=AUDIO renditions grouped and referenced by variants
A separate multivariant playlist per language
An audio track list inside each segment's metadata
The EXT-X-LANGUAGE tag on each segment
explanation: Variants name an AUDIO group; the player picks one member.

prompt: Why should segment retries use backoff and a limit?
options: Retrying tightly during an outage floods the CDN and origin
Browsers block more than one retry per URL
DRM licenses expire after one retry
Retries corrupt the SourceBuffer
explanation: Bounded retries with backoff protect infrastructure and fail clearly.

prompt: What is an origin shield?
options: A caching tier that collapses edge misses into fewer origin requests
A firewall that blocks unsigned segment URLs
A DRM wrapper around the origin
A backup origin used during failover only
explanation: It keeps many edge caches from hitting origin separately.

prompt: What is request collapsing at a CDN?
options: Merging many simultaneous misses for one object into a single origin fetch
Compressing many small segments into one response
Dropping repeated requests from the same viewer
Batching beacons before sending them
explanation: It protects origin when a new live segment is requested by everyone at once.

prompt: Why can client-side ad breaks cause black frames on some TVs?
options: Switching sources forces the decoder to tear down and reinitialize
TVs cannot decode ad codecs at all
Ad servers deliver ads without keyframes
DRM licenses must be renewed for every ad
explanation: A single stitched timeline (SSAI) avoids the source switch.

prompt: How do SSAI streams often trigger client ad beacons at the right moment?
options: Timed metadata, such as ID3 tags or date ranges, marks ad positions
The player guesses from bitrate changes
The CDN injects JavaScript into segments
The ad server calls the player directly over a persistent socket connection
explanation: EXT-X-DATERANGE or ID3 in-band metadata carries ad event timing.

prompt: In SSAI, what must a manifest signal when clear ads sit between encrypted content?
options: A discontinuity and a key change, for example EXT-X-KEY METHOD=NONE for the ads
Nothing, because players ignore encryption for ads
A new multivariant playlist for each ad
An EXT-X-ENDLIST before each ad
explanation: Players must handle both timestamp and key changes at the boundary.

prompt: What is the core trade-off of lowering live latency?
options: Less buffer means less room to absorb network jitter, so more stall risk
Lower latency always lowers video quality
Lower latency disables DRM
Lower latency makes CDN caching impossible
explanation: Latency targets trade directly against rebuffer risk.

prompt: How do players return to target latency after drifting behind live?
options: Playing slightly faster than real time for a while
Dropping every other frame
Reloading the page
Switching to the lowest rendition
explanation: hls.js and others adjust playback rate within small bounds.

prompt: Why can MPEG-TS timestamps wrap after roughly 26.5 hours?
options: PTS is a 33-bit counter at 90 kHz
Segments may not exceed one day
The HLS spec caps playlist length
The DRM license expires daily
explanation: 2^33 / 90,000 ≈ 95,443 s ≈ 26.5 h, so long live streams must handle rollover.

prompt: When does DASH SegmentTimeline beat a $Number$ template alone?
options: When segment durations vary and must be listed exactly
When all segments are the same duration
When the stream is audio only
When DRM is not used
explanation: A plain template assumes fixed durations; a timeline lists real ones.

prompt: How does a DASH live client find which segments exist?
options: It computes them from availabilityStartTime and its current wall-clock time
It downloads a full segment list each second
It asks the CDN for a directory listing
It reads the last segment's file name
explanation: Accurate client time is therefore critical for DASH live.

prompt: What is the DASH UTCTiming element for?
options: Giving clients a time source to sync their clocks
Setting the DVR window length
Declaring the license expiry
Scheduling ad breaks
explanation: Clock skew otherwise causes 404s or excess latency.

prompt: What happens if keyframes are not aligned across renditions?
options: ABR switches can glitch or require re-buffering, because boundaries differ
Only DRM playback fails
The CDN cache hit ratio drops to zero
Subtitles lose sync permanently
explanation: Aligned IDR boundaries make switching seamless.

prompt: What is per-title encoding?
options: Tuning the bitrate ladder to each title's complexity
Encoding each title with a different codec chosen by popularity
Using a different CDN for each title
Encrypting each title with its own DRM
explanation: Simple content needs fewer bits; complex content needs more.

prompt: Why keep an H.264 rendition when adding HEVC?
options: HEVC support varies across browsers and devices
H.264 is required for DRM
HEVC cannot be packaged as HLS
CDNs only cache H.264
explanation: A universally decodable fallback avoids playback failures.

prompt: What is AV1's main trade-off?
options: Better compression than H.264, at higher decode cost without hardware support
Lower quality at every bitrate
It cannot be used with DRM
It only works in Safari
explanation: Software decode of AV1 can drain battery on older devices.

prompt: A flawless-stream rate is most honest when defined over what?
options: All attempted sessions, counting startup failures as not flawless
Only sessions that reached the first frame
Only sessions longer than ten minutes
Only sessions on the highest rendition
explanation: Excluding failed starts hides the worst experiences.

prompt: Why do telemetry pipelines prefer monotonic durations over client wall-clock timestamps?
options: Device clocks drift and can be set wrong
Wall-clock time cannot be serialized
Monotonic time is smaller on the wire
Browsers block access to wall-clock time
explanation: Server receive time plus client-measured durations stays reliable.

prompt: How can a QoE pipeline detect lost or reordered events?
options: A per-session sequence number on every event
Comparing event sizes
Sorting by the device's wall clock
Asking the player to resend all of its events at the end of a session
explanation: Gaps in sequence numbers reveal loss; the order is restored downstream.

prompt: When sampling playback telemetry, what should never be sampled away?
options: Fatal error and startup failure events
Heartbeat events
Bitrate switch events
Pause events
explanation: Rare, high-signal events must be kept at 100%.

prompt: A device's DRM level forbids HD keys. How should the player behave?
options: Filter out restricted renditions so ABR never selects them
Retry the license until HD is allowed
Play HD without decryption
Stop playback with an error
explanation: Shaka calls these restrictions; unplayable tracks are removed from ABR.

prompt: Which EME session type supports offline downloads?
options: persistent-license
temporary
offline-temporary-license
cached-license
explanation: Persistent licenses are stored for later playback where supported.

prompt: How does a web app pick a DRM system with EME?
options: It calls navigator.requestMediaKeySystemAccess with key systems and configurations
It reads the DRM name from the user agent
It asks the license server which system the browser has
It tries decrypting a segment with each system
explanation: The browser returns the first supported configuration.

prompt: How should a CDN cache a live HLS media playlist?
options: With a short TTL, a fraction of the segment duration
With the same long TTL as segments
Never, since live playlists must always be fetched from the origin
For the whole DVR window
explanation: Too long a TTL makes players see stale playlists and fall behind.

prompt: What mostly drives CDN cost during a big live event?
options: Egress bandwidth, from viewers times bitrate
Number of playlist requests
Number of DRM licenses issued
Storage of live segments
explanation: Capping the top rendition is often the biggest lever.

prompt: Why pre-warm or pre-scale before a scheduled live peak?
options: Autoscaling reacts slower than a kickoff surge
Pre-warming lowers the video bitrate
CDNs refuse traffic without notice
DRM license servers need a restart before every large event
explanation: Capacity must already be there when everyone presses play.

prompt: Where should a multi-platform player share logic?
options: In a platform-neutral domain layer, keeping native playback per platform
In one web player embedded on every platform
In the backend, sending rendered frames to devices
In each platform's UI code separately
explanation: Shared state and telemetry rules, native engines underneath.

prompt: What is the risk of retrying a failed live segment for too long?
options: The playhead falls behind the live window and the segment expires
The DRM license is revoked
The CDN bans the client IP
The browser crashes
explanation: After a bounded retry, skip ahead or resync to live.
